question: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

The Commission has indicated that its intended simplification proposal known as the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus would not have a negative impact on health or the environment. On 5 March 2026, AFP reported that Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi stated that only low-risk substances were eligible for unlimited approvals. However, the current version of the text does not reflect such a restriction. Furthermore, a scientific assessment1 commissioned by the Dutch Parliament concluded that the Commission proposal fails to meet many of its intended objectives. The assessment concludes that the simplification proposal would not reduce administrative workload, risks creating an uneven playing field, could hamper innovation and poses significant risks for human and environmental health protection. 1.

Does the Commission confirm that unlimited approvals should only be granted to lowrisk substances, as defined in Article 22 of the Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in Annex 1 of Regulation (EU) No 528/2012, and that in its view the proposal should be amended to reflect this?
How does the Commission respond to the main concerns raised in the scientific assessment as described above?
Is the Commission developing its own impact assessment to evaluate these effects?

answer: (English version) to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) (12 May 2026) Subject: Impact of the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus The Commission has indicated that its intended simplification proposal known as the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus would not have a negative impact on health or the environment. On 5 March 2026, AFP reported that Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi stated that only low-risk substances were eligible for unlimited approvals. However, the current version of the text does not reflect such a restriction. Furthermore, a scientific assessment (1) commissioned by the Dutch Parliament concluded that the Commission proposal fails to meet many of its intended objectives. The assessment concludes that the simplification proposal would not reduce administrative workload, risks creating an uneven playing field, could hamper innovation and poses significant risks for human and environmental health protection. 1. Does the Commission confirm that unlimited approvals should only be granted to low-risk substances, as defined in Article 22 of the regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in Annex 1 of Regulation (EU) No 528/2012, and that in its view the proposal should be amended to reflect this? 2.
How does the Commission respond to the main concerns raised in the scientific assessment as described above?
Is the Commission developing its own impact assessment to evaluate these effects?

(3 July 2026) The Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package proposed by the Commission on 16 December 2025 (1) provides for the possibility of approvals to become unlimited for active substances except for substances that are candidates for substitution, that have been approved despite not meeting all criteria under the derogation in Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 (2) because there are no alternatives, and those for which the approval, in light of the risk assessment’s outcome, will indicate that they should be re-evaluated after a certain period of time. The Commission proposal contains safeguards to ensure that the current high level of protection of health and environment remains guaranteed, i.e. through periodic identification of active substances for a full or targeted re-evaluation (3), existing ad hoc review mechanisms and the fact that authorisations of plant protection products remain limited in time. The proposal reduces administrative burdens by streamlining procedures, clarifying and harmonising rules and allowing Member States to re-assign limited available resources from renewal procedures to the assessment of innovative substances and products. In line with one of the recommendations in the scientific assessment commissioned by the Dutch Parliament, the proposal precisely intends to achieve a ‘smarter’ reassessment system in order to address the systematic delays by proposing structural changes and recognising that significant resource increases in Member States are unlikely. The simplification proposal does not alter core policy objectives nor introduces significant new obligations, therefore, it is not accompanied by an impact assessment but a staff working document (4) analysing the expected cost savings.
